lead: Reno is high desert, but the Truckee River runs right through downtown and has flooded it more than once. Frozen pipes, snowmelt and river floods all cause water damage here.
risk: Truckee River flooding, frozen pipes and snowmelt leaks
why: On New Year's Day 1997, warm rain on deep Sierra snow sent the Truckee River out of its banks. Water spread up to two blocks from the channel and flooded downtown Reno, the airport and parts of Sparks. Damage across the region reached about $1.6 billion. In January 2017 the river hit 14.7 feet and spilled over in places, but the city was better prepared.

Winter is the more common threat. Reno sits at about 4,500 feet, and nights often drop well below freezing. Pipes in garages, crawl spaces and outside walls can freeze and split. Snow on roofs melts by day and refreezes at night, forming ice dams. Older homes in the Old Southwest and near downtown also have aging plumbing and roofs.
image_alt: Outdoor water tap dripping in a snowy yard
image_caption: Cold Reno nights can freeze and split pipes in garages and crawl spaces.
problems: Garages, crawl spaces and outside walls
Downtown and areas along the Truckee
Old Southwest and older central homes
tips: Insulate pipes in garages and crawl spaces before winter.
Keep the heat at 55°F or higher when you travel.
Disconnect hoses and cover outdoor faucets in fall.
Sign up for Truckee River flood alerts if you live near the river.
areas: Calls come from Downtown, Midtown, the Old Southwest, Northwest Reno, Somersett, Caughlin Ranch, South Meadows and Damonte Ranch, plus Sparks, Spanish Springs and Verdi.

faq.q: Do I need flood insurance in Reno's desert climate?
faq.a: If you live near the Truckee River or a wash, it is worth considering. Big floods come from warm winter storms melting snow, not just from desert rain. Home insurance does not cover rising water, and flood policies usually take 30 days to start.

sources: USGS: Flood-control effects of Truckee River reservoirs, 1997
